definition: Iridescent means showing shifting, rainbow-like colors that seem to change depending on the angle from which they're viewed.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word iridescent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know iridescent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Sunlight caught the iridescent sheen of the soap bubble just before it burst.
A shiny surface simply reflects light brightly, without necessarily changing color at all — far short of iridescent, whose rainbow colors shift with every viewing angle.
A shimmering surface flickers as light moves across it, hinting at — but not yet splitting into — the full shifting colors of something iridescent.

Opalescent evokes the soft, milky glow of an opal — pale colors floating in a cloudy stone. Iridescent is sharper and more vivid: distinct rainbow colors that flip and change as the viewing angle moves. An opal glows gently; a soap bubble flashes.

Prismatic means splitting light into the full rainbow, the way a prism throws fixed bands of color on a wall. Iridescent colors also come from bent light, but they live on a surface and shift with every change of angle rather than fanning out in fixed bands.

Lustrous describes a rich, glowing sheen — polished wood, healthy hair, satin. The shine is steady and stays one color. Iridescent surfaces do the opposite: their whole character is change, showing different colors from every new angle.

The bride chose an iridescent fabric that looked plain gray in the shop's fluorescent light but revealed flashes of purple, green, and gold the moment she stepped outside into direct sun.
The fabric wasn't dyed multiple colors — its surface simply bent light differently depending on the angle, which is precisely what makes something iridescent rather than just colorful.

Iridescent is a vivid, mostly descriptive word used for surfaces that visibly shift color with the light — soap bubbles, oil slicks, hummingbird feathers, certain fabrics and shells — not for objects that are simply multicolored or painted.

Field guides struggle with the ruby-throated hummingbird because the ruby is not always there.
Photographed from one angle, the male's throat blazes red; a step to the side and the same feathers go black.
The color is iridescent rather than pigmented: microscopic plates in each feather bend the light, and what they send back depends entirely on where you stand.
A cardinal, by contrast, is red from every seat in the yard, because its feathers carry actual red pigment.
